sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: infraction classes, amber versus red bus lights, crossbuck types, car versus truck devices, and continuation facts on work zones, crossings, trucks, motorcycles, bicycles, parking, pedestrians, belts and loads
Confusable pairs from the second half of the safe-operation chapter, followed by continuation facts the main list did not hold; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec08-R01 | anchor: A05
Not moving over for a red-light emergency vehicle is a Class A infraction, while not moving over for an amber-light parked vehicle or a disabled vehicle with hazards is a Class B infraction. [A05]
Why it matters: group Move Over; confusable infraction classes.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-R02 | anchor: A05
Amber lights on a school bus mean it is about to stop, while red lights with the stop arm come on once it has stopped. [A05]
Why it matters: group school buses; confusable amber versus red.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-R03 | anchor: A11
A disabled truck, bus or tractor-trailer must put out three bi-directional reflective triangles, or at least six fuses or three liquid-burning flares, unlike the fuse, lantern or reflector set used for a car. [A11]
Why it matters: group warning devices; confusable car versus truck.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec08-R04 | anchor: A11
In daylight a disabled car shows two red flags about 100 feet ahead and 100 feet behind, and within 500 feet of a curve or hilltop a warning device must sit at least 500 feet away. [A11]
Why it matters: group warning devices; confusable day versus night.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec08-R05 | anchor: A11
For a disabled truck, the warning device goes 200 feet away on a divided highway instead of about 100 feet. [A11]
Why it matters: group warning devices; difficulty high.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec08-R06 | anchor: A02
At some work zones, signs ask drivers to merge late toward the lane closure, known as zipper merging, to shorten the back-up. [A02]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec08-R07 | anchor: A02
Speeding into a work zone means meeting slowed or stopped traffic within seconds, so slow down and keep a safe distance on all sides. [A02]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec08-R08 | anchor: A02
The required railroad stop does not apply at abandoned tracks marked with signs or where the tracks across the road have been removed. [A02]
Why it matters: group railroad crossings; difficulty high.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec08-R09 | anchor: A03
Where there is more than one track, after one train clears make sure another train is not coming on the other track or from the opposite direction. [A03]
Why it matters: group railroad crossings; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-R10 | anchor: A03
Do not pass another vehicle within 100 feet of a railroad crossing. [A03]
Why it matters: group railroad crossings; link to no-passing rules.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-R11 | anchor: A03
Where trains run in the middle of a street, traffic signals flash red in every direction when a train approaches, and drivers treat that like any crossing warning. [A03]
Why it matters: group railroad crossings; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-R12 | anchor: A03
In local quiet zones, approaching trains do not sound their horns at some gated crossings. [A03]
Why it matters: group railroad crossings; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-R13 | anchor: A03
Without a special permit, a vehicle may be at most eight feet six inches wide, 13 feet 6 inches high and 80,000 pounds. [A03]
Why it matters: group vehicle size; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-R14 | anchor: A04
A tractor-trailer's rear wheels track a shorter path than its front wheels, so its driver often swings wide first to make a tight turn. [A04]
Why it matters: group trucks; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-R15 | anchor: A04
Cutting in front of a tractor-trailer to reach an exit removes its safety cushion; slow down and exit behind it instead. [A04]
Why it matters: group trucks; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-R16 | anchor: A04
Because of their size, tractor-trailers often look slower than they are, and many car-truck crashes at intersections happen when drivers misjudge how close a truck is. [A04]
Why it matters: group trucks; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-R17 | anchor: A06
Motorcycle turn signals usually do not cancel themselves, so wait until the rider actually starts to turn before you proceed. [A06]
Why it matters: group motorcycles; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-R18 | anchor: A06
Bicyclists may ride no more than two abreast except on paths or lanes set aside for bicycles, and they may use either the bike lane or the travel lane. [A06]
Why it matters: group bicycles; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-R19 | anchor: A06
School buses stop at railroad crossings, and rear-end crashes into buses stopped there have increased. [A06]
Why it matters: group school buses; link to railroad crossings.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-R20 | anchor: A07
Do not drive or park in a bike lane, do not move into it to prepare for a turn, and cross it only when turning or entering or leaving an alley, driveway or private road. [A07]
Why it matters: group bicycles; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-R21 | anchor: A07
After parking, check for bicyclists before you open a car door. [A07]
Why it matters: group bicycles; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-R22 | anchor: A07
Green pavement may mark a bike lane, while red pavement may mark a lane for buses, taxis or other public transit. [A07]
Why it matters: group lane markings; confusable green versus red pavement.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-R23 | anchor: A07
A sharrow is a pavement marking of a bike with two arrows that helps cyclists stay clear of parked cars and tells drivers to expect cyclists in the lane. [A07]
Why it matters: group lane markings; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-R24 | anchor: A08
To parallel park, line up beside the car ahead of the space at least two feet away with rear bumpers even, back until you reach a 45-degree angle, then turn the wheel left and straighten in the space. [A08]
Why it matters: group parking; sequence item.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-R25 | anchor: A08
Parking is also prohibited on highways unless allowed, on bridges and in tunnels, and in disability spaces without a valid placard. [A08]
Why it matters: group parking; difficulty low.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-R26 | anchor: A09
The striped area beside an accessible space is kept clear so a wheelchair user can transfer or deploy a vehicle ramp, and parking there is banned even with a valid placard. [A09]
Why it matters: group parking; link to placard rules.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-R27 | anchor: A09
Never make a turn that forces a pedestrian to stop, slow down or take special effort to avoid you. [A09]
Why it matters: group pedestrians; difficulty low.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-R28 | anchor: A09
Wear the seat belt low on the hips and flat across the collarbone, and sit at least 12 inches from the steering wheel. [A09]
Why it matters: group seat belts; difficulty medium.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-R29 | anchor: A09
Belts worn by the driver and front-seat passenger raise the chance of surviving a crash by 45 percent and cut serious injury risk by 50 percent. [A09]
Why it matters: group seat belts; difficulty low.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-R30 | anchor: A10
A person excused from a seat belt for medical reasons needs written documentation from a physician. [A10]
Why it matters: group seat belts; exemption item.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec08-R31 | anchor: A10
Where there is a passenger-side air bag, the National Safety Council advises seating children younger than 12 in the back seat. [A10]
Why it matters: group child safety; confusable with the under-eight restraint law.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec08-R32 | anchor: A11
A load or tailgate sticking out more than four feet past the rear needs a red lamp visible from 500 feet at night and a red flag of at least 12 square inches by day. [A11]
Why it matters: group loads; difficulty high.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec08-R33 | anchor: A11
If your car breaks down, turn on its hazard lights if it has them, even when you have pulled onto the shoulder. [A11]
Why it matters: group warning devices; difficulty low.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0062]

corpus_stability.reason: The Indiana Driver's Manual back cover reads Published July 2026 and tells readers to check IN.gov/BMV for updates; the BMV manual page says printed manuals are updated at most once a year, so the selected pages are treated as stable within a year while fees and service details stay dynamic.
